source.excerpt: Quality comes not from inspection, but from improvement of the production process.
trail: Quote Investigator has no article on this line, so the anchor is Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗, which lists the exact wording under Out of the Crisis with the cite “p. 29.”
A second, independent Deming quotation wiki gives the same book and page — Motley Bytes ↗ cites “Out Of The Crisis. The MIT Press. (2e ed. 1986) p. 29.”

The W. Edwards Deming Institute ↗ independently cites page 29 for the adjacent inspection passage — corroborating the page number, though the Institute does not tie that page to a numbered Point. It separately places the numbered points themselves, Point 3 included, at pages 23–24 ↗.

The book is real and datable: Open Library’s record ↗ gives MIT Center for Advanced Engineering Study, 1986, 507 pages, ISBN 0-911379-01-0, with an original date of 1982; Wikipedia ↗ notes the 1982 Quality, Productivity, and Competitive Position was renamed Out of the Crisis in 1986.
source.excerptNote: We show the sentence alone rather than stitching a longer passage together: the book is in copyright, and the surrounding sentences are quoted with slightly different page cites by different compilers. What is firmly established for page 29 is this line (per Wikiquote ↗) and, on the same page, “Inspection does not improve the quality, nor guarantee quality. Inspection is too late. The quality, good or bad, is already in the product” (per the Deming Institute ↗).

author.name: W. Edwards Deming
author.heading: Who was W. Edwards Deming?
author.bio: Deming was an American statistician who spent June to August 1950 training Japanese engineers, managers and scholars in statistical process control — work so consequential that the Union of Japanese Scientists and Engineers established the Deming Prize in December 1950, funded because Deming had declined royalties on the transcripts of his lectures. He was largely unknown to American management until the 1980s, when his 14 Points for Management reframed quality as a property of the system rather than of the finished item. This line is the compressed statement of that whole argument.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is sound — this really is Deming. What travels badly is the wording, and what part of his book it comes from.

items.who: “…but from the improvement of the production process”
items.why: An extra definite article is widely inserted; Goodreads carries this form ↗, while Wikiquote’s sourced text ↗ has plain “from improvement.”

items.who: “Quality does not come from inspection, but from improvement of the process”
items.why: A compressed restatement that circulates in management summaries of the 14 Points — for example in this fourteen-points library entry ↗, which gives no page or edition.

Point 3 as published reads “Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality. Eliminate the need for inspection on a mass basis by building quality into the product in the first place” — cited by the Deming Institute to pages 23–24 ↗. Our sentence is Deming’s explanatory prose further on.

items.who: Deming coined “You cannot inspect quality into a product”
items.why: The sibling slogan is routinely credited to Deming, but Deming credited it to the Bell Labs statistician Harold F. Dodge — quoting his own text saying so ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence itself is Deming’s, written in his own book: Out of the Crisis, page 29, per Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ and corroborated by the Deming Institute’s citation of that same page ↗.

context.heading: Why the line matters
lead: Before Deming, quality control in most Western factories meant sorting: build the batch, then inspect it and pull out the bad ones. Deming’s argument was that this is arithmetic, not improvement — the defects have already been paid for by the time an inspector finds them. The sentence on page 29 is the hinge of Point 3 of the 14 Points ↗: stop depending on inspection, and build quality in instead.

Deming had made the case in Japan decades earlier. He spent June to August 1950 training Japanese engineers, managers and scholars in statistical process control, and in December of that year the Union of Japanese Scientists and Engineers established the Deming Prize ↗ — funded because he had refused royalties on his lecture transcripts.
context.detailsSummary: How Point 3 actually reads — and what Deming credited to someone else
detailsBody: The famous sentence is Deming’s prose gloss, not the numbered point. Point 3 as published reads: “Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality. Eliminate the need for inspection on a mass basis by building quality into the product in the first place,” which the Deming Institute cites to pages 23–24 ↗.

The pull-quote above is also Deming, from the same page 29 — the Institute quotes it as “Inspection does not improve the quality, nor guarantee quality. Inspection is too late. The quality, good or bad, is already in the product.” See the Institute’s entry ↗.
The adjacent slogan “You cannot inspect quality into a product” is not Deming’s coinage — he credited it to the Bell Labs statistician Harold F. Dodge, as Michael Bolton documents ↗.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section lists "Quality comes not from inspection, but from improvement of the production process." under Out of the Crisis with the citation p. 29; the same section carries a p. 139 quote about mass inspection.
A Deming quotation wiki cites the exact wording to W. Edwards Deming (1982) Out Of The Crisis, The MIT Press, 2e ed. 1986, p. 29.

The W. Edwards Deming Institute cites Out of the Crisis page 29 for "Inspection does not improve the quality, nor guarantee quality. Inspection is too late. The quality, good or bad, is already in the product." — and page 227 for "Quality can not be inspected into a product or service; it must be built into it." It does not carry the "Quality comes not from inspection" phrasing.

The Deming Institute gives Point 3 as "Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality. Eliminate the need for inspection on a mass basis by building quality into the product in the first place," cited to Out of The Crisis (MIT Press), pages 23-24.

Goodreads carries the variant wording "Inspection to improve quality is too late, ineffective, costly. Quality comes not from inspection, but from the improvement of the production process," credited to Out of the Crisis.
A fourteen-points library entry renders the idea as the paraphrase "Quality does not come from inspection, but from improvement of the process," without citing an edition or page.
"You cannot inspect quality into a product" originates with Harold F. Dodge, and Deming credited Dodge for it in Out of the Crisis.

W. Edwards Deming was born 14 October 1900 and died 20 December 1993; he trained Japanese engineers and managers in statistical process control from June to August 1950; JUSE established the Deming Prize in December 1950 after he declined royalties on his lecture transcripts; the 1982 book Quality, Productivity, and Competitive Position was renamed Out of the Crisis in 1986.
Out of the Crisis catalog record: W. Edwards Deming, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Center for Advanced Engineering Study, 1986 (original 1982), 507 pages, ISBN 0-911379-01-0.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Out of the Crisis published by MIT's Center for Advanced Engineering Study, 1986, access-restricted (lending).
